result:
I'll write about dead reckoning, which I've always found quietly wonderful.

Before satellites, and before clocks good enough to solve longitude, a ship out of sight of land found its position by arithmetic. You began at the last place you were sure of. The compass gave your heading, a sandglass gave the time elapsed, and for speed you used a piece of wood on a rope. This was the chip log, a weighted board tossed off the stern that stayed more or less put in the water while the ship sailed away from it, pulling out a line knotted at regular intervals. A sailor counted the knots slipping through his hands until the glass ran out, which is why ships' speeds are still given in knots.

Many crews couldn't read or write, so the record was kept on a traverse board, a wooden panel with holes radiating along the points of the compass. Every half hour of the watch, someone stuck a peg in the hole for the course steered. At the end of the watch the navigator read the pegs, averaged them, and drew a line on the chart: we are here, probably.

The "probably" is the part I like. Every error goes into the estimate and stays there: a current you can't feel, a helmsman drifting two degrees, a glass turned a moment late. Nothing inside the method corrects them, and they compound. Navigators knew this, so they seized any outside check, such as a star sight, a depth sounding, or a headland someone recognized, and started fresh from it. The skill was never in believing the estimate. It was in holding it at exactly the confidence it had earned and still steering by it, because the ship has to go somewhere.

Desert ants do the same thing. Cataglyphis ants forage across the Sahara on wandering, looping paths, over ground too hot for scent trails to last, and then walk home in a straight line. They track direction by the sky and distance, it turns out, by something like counting steps. In 2006 researchers tested this by gluing pig-bristle stilts onto ants that had just reached food. The ants on stilts marched right past their nest, while ants with shortened legs stopped short. Each had taken the right number of steps with the wrong legs.

There's a popular story that "dead reckoning" comes from "ded. reckoning," short for "deduced." It's tidy and it sounds right, but there's no real evidence for it. Nobody knows for sure where the "dead" comes from, though it may be the same one as in "dead ahead." The etymology is a plausible line drawn from a known point with nothing to check it against, so it's dead reckoning without the fix.

I'm settling on dead reckoning, the old method of estimating position from a known starting point, heading, and speed. Its appeal is that small errors pile up over distance, which makes it a good subject for a short essay. I'm also noting that the desert ant experiments with stilts show the same principle at work in a living navigator.

I'm working through the mechanics of the log: a weighted board thrown off the stern stays roughly in place while the line pays out behind it, and the knots passing through the hands during a half-minute glass give the speed. That's the origin of ships still measuring speed in knots. I'm also noting the traverse board, which let crews who couldn't read or write record their headings each half hour.

The desert ant experiment carries the same idea into living things: Cataglyphis foragers wander off across bare sand with no scent trail to follow, then head straight home, apparently by counting their steps. When researchers fitted stilts to returning ants, they overshot the nest, and when they trimmed legs, the ants fell short, which suggests the ants were measuring distance rather than sight.

The etymology is where I want to be careful: the common story that "dead" comes from "deduced" looks like a later invention, since nothing in the logbooks supports it. More likely the word is tied to "dead ahead" or "dead in the water," but nobody is certain. There's a quiet irony there, a phrase about careful inference whose own origin was filled in with a tidy, plausible account that nobody checked against a fix.

I'm settling the closing line now: the etymology irony works well as an ending, a plausible account drawn from a known point with nothing to check it against. I'm also noting the ant stilt study as a precise citation to keep, and the knot spacing detail is optional, since a half-minute glass is close enough.
